title: A second bakery on Gaston Avenue (and the SBA idea)

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Okay, so, um, the landlord on Gaston Avenue called me back. The old dry cleaner space, the one by the Lakewood Theater? He'll hold it until December first, but not a day longer.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: December first. That's, what, three and a half weeks? Marisol, we haven't even priced the build-out.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: I did price it. The contractor came Tuesday. Ovens, the hood, the walk-in cooler, the front counter, the whole thing. He said about two hundred fifty thousand for the build-out. That's with a little cushion.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Two fifty. Okay. And we'd put that on... what, exactly? We don't have that just sitting in the bank.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: No, no. That's why I called Rosa's lender, the SBA guy. The seven-a loan. Ten years, and with the bakery's numbers he thinks we'd probably qualify. We put ten percent down, maybe twenty-five thousand.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Twenty-five thousand. Which is most of the emergency fund.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Most of it, yes, I know, that's what I'm— wait, let me finish. We have fourteen thousand in the emergency fund, and October through December is our best quarter. Día de Muertos, the tamale orders, Christmas.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Best quarter, but also the lumpy one, mi amor. Remember last January? Flour, the lease, the estimated taxes all went out in one week and your draw was tiny.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Can I say something? Mom, are you gonna work even more? You're already at the shop at four in the morning.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Mija, that's fair. That's, okay, that's really fair. The idea is Lupe runs the new place. She's been with us six years. So it's not me at two ovens at once.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: Is there gonna be pan de muerto at the new one? Do I get a free concha?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Mateo, buddy, this is adult talk. We'll discuss concha policy later.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: That's not a no.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: It's not a no. Okay, Daniel, honestly, what's your gut?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: My gut is I love it and I'm scared. Um. If the second place takes, like, eight months to break even, can we still cover the mortgage and Sofia's volleyball and the truck payment? Because my paycheck covers the mortgage and not much else.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: That's what I want to run through. The bakery did about one point three million last year. If the new store does even half of that by year two--

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Even half. And if it does a third?

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Then we're tight for a year. I'm not saying it's risk free.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Okay. And how long does the SBA thing take? Because December first is soon.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: He said six to eight weeks once the paperwork is in. So we ask the landlord for a lease that starts in March, rent kicks in after the build-out, and we open by the end of September next year.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Fine. Let's do it properly. Let's find out what we'd actually be approved for and what the payment would be, then decide. I don't want to guess.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Deal. And a plan for the lumpy months. Like a bakery reserve so a slow February doesn't land on our personal checking.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Dad said deal so it's official.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: I said let's find out. Different.

title: Abuela's care and Sofia's college fund

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Mamá, sit, sit. We want to talk about the doctor stuff, and we want you in the room for it, not hearing about it later.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Ay, Marisol, I don't want to be a burden. I can pay for my own pills.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Elena, nobody said burden. Nobody. We just want to look at the real numbers together.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: So, the hospital bill in September was three thousand four hundred and twelve dollars. That was after the supplement paid. And the cardiologist copays, the pharmacy, it's adding up.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: I added it up last night. Pharmacy, the heart doctor, the aide you wanted for the mornings... it's about seven hundred eighty a month. That's roughly nine thousand a year, if nothing new happens.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Nine thousand! Dios mío. That's too much. I could use less help. I don't need somebody every day.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Mamá, you fell in the kitchen in August. The aide stays, at least three mornings a week.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Okay, okay. Three mornings. But my Social Security, I want to put something in. Not nothing.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: You already put in. Your check pays for half the groceries. Let us handle the medical for the year. I'd say let's set aside nine thousand and stop worrying about it every month.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: And Medicare open enrollment closes December seventh. I want to compare plans before then, there's one with a lower out-of-pocket max.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Good. Put that on the list, with a date.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Can I ask a question? Is this going to, like, take money from college? Because Ms. Alvarez said I should start looking at applications in two years.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: No, mija, we're not taking from your college fund. We're just being honest that everything has a cost.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: I want to study nursing, maybe. At UT Dallas or A&M. Abuela's doctors are kind of why.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Ay, mi niña. See? I told you, she has my heart. The good part, not the broken part.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Ha. Okay. So the college fund. We've got twenty-one thousand five hundred in there for you and Mateo. We put in five hundred a month.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Four years in state is, what, a hundred thousand with everything? Housing, books, all of it?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: About that. If we want sixty thousand saved by the time Sofia starts, which is August of twenty twenty-nine, we need to put in more than five hundred. Closer to eight hundred a month.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Eight hundred is a lot with the bakery being up and down.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It is. Maybe five hundred now and a lump in the busy season when the draws are fat. Every holiday quarter, we throw some in.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: I can work at the bakery on Saturdays and put that in too. Real wages. Mom, you owe me minimum wage.

turns.speaker: Marisol
turns.text: Minimum wage, I'll think about it. Okay. Sixty thousand by August of twenty twenty-nine, and nine thousand set aside for Abuela.

expected_goals.title: Set aside funds for Elena's medical and home-care costs
Compare Medicare plans for Elena before open enrollment ends Dec 7
expected_goals.evidence_quote: Medicare open enrollment closes December seventh

expected_goals.title: Grow the college fund to $60,000 by Sofia's freshman year
expected_goals.evidence_quote: sixty thousand saved by the time Sofia starts

title: Buying our first home in two years

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Okay, so, I ran the numbers on that listing site again. If we want a place around three hundred forty thousand, in like, Garland or Mesquite or Lake Highlands...

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Lake Highlands is not three-forty, babe. Lake Highlands is four-fifty for a shoebox.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Fine, Mesquite or Richardson. The point is, three-forty, five percent down is seventeen thousand, plus closing costs, call it, um, thirty thousand total to be safe.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Thirty thousand. We have, what, twenty-two in the House Fund right now?

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Twenty-two three. Which would've been twenty-seven if that weird transfer in September hadn't happened.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Don't. I'm still mad. The bank says they're still investigating, maybe a provisional credit by Thanksgiving.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Okay. Okay. But even with that, we put in six hundred a month, so, what, another year and we hit thirty. That's the easy part.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Right, so what's the hard part?

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: The cards. The loan officer told me, like, bluntly, with our utilization we'd get a worse rate and maybe not even get approved. Mine's at like eighty-six percent.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Eighty-six. Ugh. Mine's the store card, that's sixty-one. And that stupid Southwest flight is still on yours.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: It's the flight and the dining and, honestly, DoorDash. Don't look at me like that, you ordered half of it.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: I ordered... okay, I ordered half of it.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: So the plan is, we get both cards under thirty percent before we apply. That's about, um, sixty-eight hundred we'd have to pay down.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Sixty-eight hundred. While also saving six hundred a month. On top of two student loans, the Civic, rent at seventeen twenty-five...

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: I know. It's a stretch. But if we cut the Peloton and the DoorDash habit, that's like three hundred a month right there.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: The Peloton is the only thing keeping me alive.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Crunch is twenty-five dollars, Chidi.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Fine. Fine. Cancel the Peloton. What about an emergency fund? If we put everything into the house and then the AC dies in our new place...

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: Good point. Three months of bare-bones expenses is, um, like fifteen thousand. That's separate from the House Fund.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Fifteen. So really we're saving forty-five total. In two years. On two incomes. Okay. That sounds scary when you say it out loud.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: It's scary but it's also one number at a time. Cards first, then the House Fund, then the emergency fund. Our lease is up in October of twenty twenty-eight, so that's the target.

turns.speaker: Chidi
turns.text: Okay. October twenty twenty-eight. Write it on the fridge.

expected_goals.title: Buy a first home by October 2028
expected_goals.evidence_quote: thirty thousand total to be safe

expected_goals.title: Get both credit cards under 30% utilization before applying for a mortgage
expected_goals.evidence_quote: we get both cards under thirty percent before we apply

title: The phone call about Kevin

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: Okay, Ba, Má, start from the beginning. Slowly. What time did the phone ring?

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Um, about noon. Maybe twelve-thirty? Wednesday. The phone said Houston, so I thought maybe it was Kevin's school.

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: A man said, Grandma? It's me. Very quiet, crying a little. I said Kevin? And he said yes.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: Má, you said his name first. Okay, keep going.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Then another man took the phone. He said he was Attorney Mark Whitfield. Kevin had a car accident, the police found something in the car, and Kevin was in the county jail.

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: He said bail was two thousand dollars, and it had to be today, or Kevin would stay in jail over the weekend.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: And he said do not tell Kevin's mom and dad, because Kevin was embarrassed and the case could be sealed if we paid fast.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: And you paid how?

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: He said the court takes gift cards because the computer system was down. So I went to CVS, and then Walgreens. Tom took the car to Target and Kroger.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Five hundred each, four stores. The man stayed on the phone with me the whole time. He told me which cards, Apple and Google Play and Target, and to read him the numbers on the back.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: The whole time? Ba, did the cashier say anything?

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: The girl at Walgreens asked if it was a gift. The man said say yes. I said yes.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Then he called again Thursday. He said Kevin needed three thousand five hundred more for court fees. That's when Linh said wait.

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: I said, I want to talk to Kevin. He said no, Kevin has no phone. I hung up. My hands were shaking.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: I'm so glad you hung up. I called Kevin an hour ago. He's at work in Houston. He's fine. He's never been arrested.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Two thousand dollars.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: I know. Ba, it's not your fault. These people are professionals. They find the grandchildren's names online.

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: And then somebody called who said IRS. Saying we owe back taxes and there is a warrant. That time I knew. I knew.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: Okay. Here's what we do. Tomorrow we go to the bank branch and report the debit card purchases. We call the gift card companies with the numbers, sometimes they can freeze unspent cards. We file a police report and one with the FTC. And we put alerts on all your accounts.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: And a rule for the house. Any call about money, we hang up and call the family back on the number we already know.

turns.speaker: Linh
turns.text: A code word. With Kevin. Something only family knows.

turns.speaker: Mai
turns.text: Yes. Also, Ba, the six-month CD at the bank, it matures December fifth. We should decide before then what to do with it. Don't let anyone talk you into moving it.

expected_goals.title: Report the $2,000 gift-card scam and try to recover the money
Turn on scam alerts and a call-back rule for every account
expected_goals.evidence_quote: we put alerts on all your accounts

expected_goals.title: Decide what to do with the 6-month CD maturing Dec 5

scam_signals: Caller posed as a grandchild in jail and begged them not to tell his parents
Second caller posed as an attorney and set a same-day deadline for $2,000 bail
Payment demanded in gift cards (Apple, Google Play, Target) with card numbers read out over the phone
Caller stayed on the line during the purchases and coached the answer to the cashier
Four $500 gift-card purchases at four stores within about two hours (13:04 to 15:02 on Oct 21)
Follow-up call the next day demanded $3,500 more for 'court fees'
Caller refused to let them speak to the grandson directly
A separate call impersonating the IRS threatened a warrant over back taxes

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Okay, Neha, I'm putting you on speaker, I'm just doing the math in the car real quick. Aarav, seatbelt.

turns.speaker: Neha
turns.text: Go. What's the damage?

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: So. Bank app says a hundred sixty-four dollars. The installment loan comes out Tuesday, that's one forty-two. Insurance is Friday morning, one forty-eight. And my paycheck is not until Friday the thirteenth. It posts in the afternoon, of course.

turns.speaker: Neha
turns.text: So wait, you're short? Before Friday?

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Not short short. Tuesday is the DoorDash payout, it's usually like two hundred. But if it's a slow week, um, it's like ninety, and then something bounces and they hit me with the thirty-five dollar overdraft fee. Again.

turns.speaker: Neha
turns.text: Again? How many times since the summer?

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: I counted. Twelve. Twelve times since May. That's 420 dollars gone, that's most of a car payment.

turns.speaker: Aarav
turns.text: Mom, can I get the thing from the machine? The claw machine?

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Not today, baby. Mommy's counting. Sit tight.

turns.speaker: Aarav
turns.text: You're always counting.

turns.speaker: Neha
turns.text: Priya, let me send you something. A hundred.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: No, no. I'm not-- okay. Honestly? Just for the rent thing. I was late in October and they charged seventy-five.

turns.speaker: Neha
turns.text: Take it. Pay me back whenever. But you need a cushion. Like, anything. Five hundred dollars that's just there.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: A five hundred dollar cushion. By January. I would cry. Okay. Every payout, I take fifteen percent and don't touch it. DoorDash, Uber, Instacart. Fifteen percent goes in the savings account.

turns.speaker: Neha
turns.text: And the bank app thing, with the weird charges, the garbled ones?

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Yeah, the import is a mess. There's a coffee that says ten million dollars. I'm not even kidding. I need to get that sorted before I ever try to get a better loan.

expected_goals.title: Make it to Friday's paycheck without an overdraft
expected_goals.evidence_quote: my paycheck is not until Friday the thirteenth

expected_goals.title: Save 15% of every gig payout
expected_goals.evidence_quote: Every payout, I take fifteen percent and don't touch it

title: The roof, Pop's care, and Jordan's college money

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Okay, family meeting. Jordan, phone down. Terrence, you too. Pop, do you want your tea before we start?

turns.speaker: Walter
turns.text: I'm fine, Danielle. Go ahead. I'll just listen and pretend I'm not eavesdropping.

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: So, three things. The roof, the aide for Pop, and Jordan's college money. And I want us to talk about it as one budget, not three arguments.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Roof first, since it leaked again. The guy said patching the section over the garage is a Band-Aid. A full replacement is, um, fourteen thousand five hundred.

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: We did the storm repair in September for twenty-eight sixty. That was supposed to hold.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: It held for six weeks. He says get it done before spring storm season, April at the latest.

turns.speaker: Jordan
turns.text: Can I say something about the car thing?

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: Jordan, we haven't even gotten to the car thing.

turns.speaker: Jordan
turns.text: I'm just saying, I'll be seventeen in March, I have like twenty-one hundred saved from Zaxby's, and I'm on the schedule for thirty hours over Christmas.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Baby, we'll get there. College first.

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: Okay. The 529. We have twenty-seven four in there and we put in four-fifty a month. Jordan starts fall of twenty twenty-eight. To cover about sixty thousand, we're, um, twenty-some thousand short.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Twenty-some thousand. On top of the roof.

turns.speaker: Walter
turns.text: Can I put my two cents in, since I'm apparently a line item?

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: Pop, you're not a line item.

turns.speaker: Walter
turns.text: I am, and that's fine. The aide is six forty a month. I'd rather that money went to Jordan's school than me sitting around with company. Cut it to once a week.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Absolutely not. You fell in June. The aide stays.

turns.speaker: Walter
turns.text: Then at least let me put an extra two hundred a month toward the college thing out of my Social Security.

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: ...Okay. Okay, Pop. Thank you. That helps.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: So I think the roof comes first, because water in the house costs more than anything. Our mortgage is three point four, so I'm not touching that with a refinance.

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: No refinance. The emergency fund has eleven eight, a roof at fourteen five would take all of it and then some. I'd rather save over five months, about three thousand a month, and get the roof on in April.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Three thousand a month. Tight, but the raise kicks in January.

turns.speaker: Jordan
turns.text: What if I just drive the old Corolla? I don't need a new car. I need, like, a car.

turns.speaker: Walter
turns.text: That Corolla is in the shop more than on the road. Eight thousand five hundred gets you something decent with low miles.

turns.speaker: Terrence
turns.text: Jordan, I'll match whatever you save, up to four thousand. The rest we revisit in June.

turns.speaker: Jordan
turns.text: Deal. Wait, really? Deal.

turns.speaker: Danielle
turns.text: Write it down: roof by April, the 529 gets Pop's two hundred plus our four-fifty, and Jordan's car by June.

expected_goals.title: Replace the roof before spring storm season
expected_goals.evidence_quote: A full replacement is, um, fourteen thousand five hundred

expected_goals.title: Close the gap on Jordan's 529 before fall 2028
